title: Kula Disaster Recovery Update Meeting of November 16, 2023

recap.headline: Kula fire debris cleanup, air and soil testing worries, and Upcountry water
recap.in_60_seconds: Mayor Bissen, Maui Emergency Management, the Army Corps of Engineers, the State Department of Health and County water staff held a recovery update for Kula fire-area residents. About 12 residents spoke. Officials said two cleanup crews are working, a third will start once five rights of entry clear, and owners get at least 72 hours' notice. Residents pressed for better air monitoring, soil tests on neighboring yards and health screening; the Health Department said its request to FEMA for neighbor soil testing is still pending, and it will look into subsidizing blood and urine tests. The weekly Kula meetings will move to Tuesdays, and EPA is expected at the next one.

parts.title: Opening and meeting schedule
presented: Kula updates will be held weekly, like the Wednesday Lahaina meetings
A show of hands moved the Kula meetings from Thursdays to Tuesdays
Not all resource people could attend this first meeting

parts.title: Emergency management update on notices
presented: Owners get no less than 72 hours' notice before debris removal
Staff go door to door and leave door hangers listing the address scheduled and phone numbers
Neighbors are also notified when a nearby lot is scheduled

parts.title: Army Corps debris removal update
parts.presenter: Army Corps of Engineers debris specialist
presented: One lot awaits soil sample results and another awaits a closeout report
Air monitoring on site has been good
Work stopped one day after a contractor employee died in an off-site traffic accident, and to tighten fall protection
FEMA ruled that neighboring properties with blown ash are not eligible for the cleanup program

next.what: Explain why one owner did not get notice of work

parts.title: Department of Health air and ash update
parts.presenter: State Department of Health Deputy Director of Environmental Health
presented: Lahaina ash sampling is done; results expected in about three weeks
57 PurpleAir sensors and E-BAM monitors are on Maui and Lānaʻi, including 25 PurpleAir sensors and 6 E-BAMs in Kula
A contractor started Kula air monitoring last week, with daily sampling for asbestos and metals like arsenic, lead and chromium
The Department asked FEMA to test soil and ash on properties next to burned homes

raised.concern: Residents cannot learn which lots will be cleared or plan around work announced the night before.

answered.said: Two crews are working; a third starts once five rights of entry are released. The contractor sets the order and gives 72 hours' notice; work is likely within about three days.
Schedules can be posted on the MauiRecovers website, and staff ask for the information daily.

raised.concern: Low-cost PurpleAir sensors do not measure heavy metals; residents want EPA-grade monitors in Kula and public data after three months with little monitoring.
A local industrial hygienist said home exposure should follow HUD rather than OSHA standards, mercury vapor should be tested, local experts have not been used, and it is unclear who is in charge.
A stand-down after a worker death should be required, not optional.
People, not just air, should be tested for exposure.

answered.said: Ash is about 0.3% arsenic, so dust readings give an idea of airborne arsenic; dust tracked indoors is the bigger risk, so keep homes clean.

answered.who: Department of Health Hazard Evaluation and Emergency Response staff
answered.said: E-BAMs are the same type EPA used in August; 24-hour lab sampling for metals and asbestos is under way and results will be made public; PurpleAir sensors are placed next to E-BAMs to check them.
Metals in ash are airborne only with dust, earlier EPA sampling found no elevated metals, EPA data is posted, and new debris-removal sampling results will be made public.

next.what: Post results of new air sampling during debris removal

parts.title: Residents' cleanup experience and neighbor soil testing

raised.concern: A fire survivor and a neighbor said crews wet the ground constantly and no dust rose, even on a windy day.
A neighbor of burned homes who became ill was denied FEMA help twice and asked why yards next to burned lots cannot be tested.

answered.said: He helped her through every request process and has reached the limit of what the debris mission can do.
The mission already covers more than ever, including cars, vessels and soil sampling; health risk from blown ash is for the Department of Health and the State.
Wash hands and clean homes; the request to FEMA to test neighbors' soil is still pending; owners may hire their own contractor to test.
He will track where the request stands and look for local testing resources for properties not eligible under FEMA.

next.what: Follow up on the Health Department's request to FEMA for neighbor soil testing

parts.title: Questions on ash data and children's health

raised.concern: Ash results were pooled from eight sites; a neighbor wants each burned lot sampled because homes and contents vary widely.
Residents want the same exposure monitoring cleanup workers wear.
A parent asked what data shows children near burned lots are safe, noting no Kula monitors for seven weeks, and whether the State would subsidize blood and urine testing.

answered.said: One composite sample from 240 points at eight of 20-plus burned homes showed high arsenic; testing each lot is possible but not the office's plan, and arsenic drives the risk.
Worker monitor questions are for EPA, which they will try to bring to the next meeting.

Talk to a health provider: blood tests for lead and urine tests for arsenic; a medical advisory went to providers; no new exposure is believed since soil tack was applied; subsidizing testing will be looked into.

next.what: Look into subsidizing blood and urine testing
More outreach so providers get the medical advisory

raised.concern: How much water is left Upcountry and what is the backup plan.
Backup generators at pump stations are still not installed.
Burn-area residents need water to wash down ash and keep hydroseeded lots watered despite restrictions.
How the proposed three-tier water rate with irrigation would work.

answered.said: Reservoirs are at 60% and 45% and filling; wells at Hāmākua Poko are being tested for use if needed.
Generators are not acquired yet; more funding is being sought.
Burned and neighboring properties may use water if owners give their locations.
The three-tier proposal has not passed and is still going through.

parts.title: Final concerns and wrap-up
presented: Rights of entry stalled over conflicting reports between the County and the right-of-entry contractor
Schedules will be shared through community networks and County recovery websites; work will not start sooner than 72 hours but may slip

raised.concern: Hot spots still smoke in the gulch, and a visitor claiming to be sent by the Governor took photos and refused to sign in.
Some rights of entry have not reached the Army Corps.
Smoke and ash from the still-burning gulch affect residents' lungs well outside the burn area.

answered.said: County, Corps and contractor officials will meet in the morning to fix the right-of-entry problem; he does not know which five lots are affected.
He will take her location and share it with the response team to look at wider community impacts.

next.what: County, Army Corps and contractor meeting on rights of entry
EPA to attend and speak on monitoring
Post debris schedules on County recovery websites

bills.name: Proposed three-tier water rate
bills.what: A proposed County water rate structure including irrigation water, not yet passed.

votes.what: Show of hands on moving Kula meetings from Thursdays to Tuesdays
votes.result: Mayor said meetings will move to Tuesdays

open_questions.question: Why did FEMA deny cleanup for properties next to burned lots?
Will FEMA approve the Health Department's request to test soil and ash on neighboring properties?
Will the State subsidize blood and urine testing for exposed residents?
What do cleanup workers' monitors detect, and can the community get the same monitoring?
Is mercury vapor being tested for?
When will backup generators be installed at Upcountry pump stations?

moments.quote: Okay, so right now, the reservoirs are filling and that's good. So one of our reservoirs is at 60 percent, the other one is at 45 percent.
moments.about: Gives the Upcountry reservoir levels during the water shortage in November 2023.

moments.quote: Okay, so we're trying to clear some of our wells at Hamakua Popo to use that if we need to.
moments.about: Names the backup plan of bringing wells at Hāmākua Poko online if Upcountry water runs short.

moments.quote: Well, we will be willing to let those people with, to have those properties that were burnt, or next to properties that are burnt, use the water.
moments.about: Says burned properties and their neighbors can get an exception to water-use limits to control ash, if they tell the department where they are.

moments.who: A Kula resident near the burn area
moments.quote: You kind of already answered it, but the request I know has been received for people that are still dealing with burn-affected properties and if they can be exempted from the water situations right now, like when Army Corps goes through and hydro-seeds properties at the end, our understanding is that's the responsibility of the property owner to keep that irrigated.
moments.about: Explains why fire-affected property owners need an exemption from Upcountry water restrictions to keep reseeded lots watered.
